articles.title: Meet the MIT students who built a system that turns lunar waste into useful materials for future Moon missions, winning both tracks of NASA’s LunaRecycle Challenge and $925,000 in prizes
articles.summary: The Moon has a few things in common with Earth. No, we’re not talking about craters or imperfections, but trash.
articles.body: The Moon has a few things in common with Earth. No, we’re not talking about craters or imperfections, but trash. Building a home for humans on the Moon is a dream that many scientists are working to make a reality. But as supplies arrive from Earth, so will packaging and other waste. With astronauts also needing tools and spare parts to maintain their lunar base, an MIT student team has developed a system that turns lunar waste into useful materials. The student team CERBERUZ has won both tracks of NASA’s LunaRecycle Centennial Challenge and $925,000 in prize money.Trash that has nowhere to goThe future lunar base will receive a steady stream of supplies, most of which will arrive wrapped in material that gets tossed once opened. The base will also need tools, spare parts and building materials. George Lordos, a research scientist at MIT and the team’s lead adviser, says that waste will keep building up while maintenance demands new materials. Turning trash into useful materials means fewer items have to be launched from Earth.“Waste packaging materials will inevitably accumulate when a lunar outpost is built, and at the same time, outpost construction and maintenance will require a steady supply of new materials, including replacement parts. Recycling waste materials into such parts can help reduce the materials needed to be launched from Earth,” said Lordos, a research scientist in MIT’s Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics and System Design and Management, in a statement.Now the million-dollar question: how do they turn this waste into useful materials for lunar living? The system splits non-biological waste into two groups: plastics that melt when heated and everything else. All of it is ground into a fine powder and mixed together. That powder goes into an injection moulding machine, where the plastics melt and hold the other pieces in place. The mixture is pushed into a mould, producing a solid part that can be made again and again.Recycling the impossibleThe team even recycled something that nobody knew how to recycle. The material in question is Zotek F30, a lightweight foam used in aerospace packaging. Mixed plastics and foams like it have no proven recycling method, even on Earth. CERBERUZ takes a different route, mixing the foam into the melted material as a filler. The catch is that it weighs almost nothing. José Soto, a graduate student and the team’s pre-processing lead, said, “We had big shipments of Zotek coming in, and one person can carry them on their head like it’s nothing. The box is the size of a person.”Designed for life far from EarthLanie McKinney, a graduate student who leads the team, says the system had to work within strict limits. “We set out to build something that would actually make sense on the Moon, not just in a lab,” said McKinney, a graduate student in AeroAstro and team lead for CERBERUZ. “That means no water and no chemicals you can’t replace. Every design choice we made was driven by those constraints. And we don’t want to recycle just for recycling’s sake; we want to make useful things. Part of how we framed the problem was to create a system that can process nearly any feedstock and turn it into a wide array of components, giving more utility than producing a single item.”The team also built DEIMOS, short for Digital Environment for Intelligent Modeling of Operational Systems, alongside the hardware. It is a digital copy of the moulding machine, built from data collected during real production runs. It predicts how a given mix of recycled material and part shape will fill the mould, warp and shrink. Before astronauts spend scarce materials on a part, they could test it on a computer first.Winning the $925,000 challengeThe team grew out of the MIT Space Resources Workshop, a student group founded in 2017 that builds systems for future Moon and Mars missions. CERBERUZ draws students from four departments: Aeronautics and Astronautics, Mechanical Engineering, Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, and Materials Science and Engineering. Professor Jeffrey Hoffman, a former NASA astronaut, advised the team alongside Lordos.The team was named a Phase 1 winner in 2025, progressed through Phase 2 and earned milestone prizes in both tracks before the final demonstration in summer 2026. The prize money totalled $925,000.“If we’re able to reduce the amount of waste that’s inevitably going to be left on the Moon, rather than letting it pile up like a landfill, we can preserve both the beauty of the Moon and make exploration more efficient and sustainable. And perhaps we can inspire people back on Earth to take another look at our trash and find more ways to recycle or reuse it,” Soto concluded.

articles.title: Elon Musk says Ukraine’s military violated Starlink’s terms of service
articles.summary: Elon Musk says Ukraine’s military violated Starlink’s terms of service by using it to carry out offensive drone strikes. The statement comes nearly two weeks after Ukrainian officials accused SpaceX of throttling the military’s satellite internet service.
articles.body: Elon Musk claims Ukraine violated Starlink’s terms of service before the recent slowdown, as reported earlier by Ars Technica. According to Musk, “Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week,” however Ukrainian officials have denied that happened, or that it is actually possible for them to do. The statement comes nearly two weeks after Ukrainian officials accused SpaceX of putting limits on the military’s satellite internet service that disrupted its drone missions and operations. As reported by Axios, Ukraine uses Starlink for communications, logistics, and to defend against incoming drones. For offensive missions, officials say that Ukraine uses Starshield, the US military-controlled variant of Starlink. Musk points to a post from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, which said Ukraine uses “Starlink from mid-range strikes against enemy military targets,” in violation of Starlink’s policies. However, Serhii Beskrestnov, a defense technology advisor for Zelenskyy, pushed back on this in a post on Telegram, saying Starlink’s systems can only connect to devices traveling between 70 and 90 kilometers per hour (around 43 and 55 miles per hour) and don’t work in Russia. “Therefore, we physically cannot use commercial Starlink for deep strikes or medium-range strikes,” Beskrestnov wrote. Ars Technica also points out a tweet from another former Ukrainian advisor, Serhii Sternenko, that went into more detail, saying that while stationary terminals could be registered (with Starlink) by military personnel or civilians, “for any satellite terminal to work while on the move, it had to be added to a special list and connected to the military Starshield system… In other words, using civilian Starlink for drone missions was technically impossible. All drone missions that required satellite communication could only be carried out using Starshield.” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Saturday that Starlink and Starshield services had been fully restored. With the restriction lifted, Ukraine’s military can now connect to devices traveling at speeds of more than 400kmh (248mph), the Kyiv Independent reports. Though Musk initially offloaded the blame for the slowdown in Ukraine onto the US government, President Donald Trump responded by saying he “wasn’t involved” and didn’t know who throttled SpaceX’s services. A report from The Wall Street Journal later said Trump asked Musk to lift restrictions on Ukraine.

articles.title: ​Meet Kayley Xu, a San Diego student who developed Aucura, a wearable stethoscope designed to improve respiratory diagnostics, and won a $25,000 national entrepreneurship prize
articles.summary: Kayley Xu, a Year 12 student from San Diego, won the $25,000 grand prize in the Mott Million Dollar Challenge for developing Aucura, a wearable
articles.body: Kayley Xu, a Year 12 student from San Diego, won the $25,000 grand prize in the Mott Million Dollar Challenge for developing Aucura, a wearable stethoscope designed to improve respiratory diagnostics. The device aims to capture and analyse sounds from the body to help identify breathing-related problems. Xu hopes to make the technology affordable enough to reach rural communities and underfunded clinics, where access to medical equipment can be limited. “I’m really grateful for experiences like these, as they’re really formative in helping young people like me decide what they want to do in the future,” Xu told the Mott Foundation.It all started with pneumoniaThe idea for Aucura came to Kayley Xu a few months after she recovered from pneumonia. The wearable device is designed to improve auscultation, the process of listening to sounds inside the body, and help advance respiratory diagnostics. “It’s often done using a stethoscope. This process has existed for over 200 years, but the device itself, the traditional stethoscope, has remained relatively unchanged over that time, which is another part of why I was really motivated to advance this technology,” she explained.Xu first tried to solve the problem with software alone. That approach hit a wall quickly because the hardware was not advanced enough to produce useful data. So she shifted her focus to building a sturdier chest piece, the part of the stethoscope that rests against the body. Only then did she turn to the software that would interpret the sounds and turn them into information a doctor could use.While designing Aucura, she spoke to many professionals, including doctors. “I talked to my paediatric physician about the idea. She was able to look at some of the chest pieces I designed and gave me feedback on them. That validated my idea early on,” Xu recalled.Testing the deviceTesting a medical device on live patients wasn’t easy for the California teen. “I wanted to test Aucura in real life, and it’s kind of hard to do in vitro tests or tests in live human patients.” So instead, she made something in her kitchen. “I created a model of the human torso using foamed gelatine.”She mixed gelatine powder and water, then whipped the mixture with an electric mixer, the same kind people use for baking. She moulded the foam into a model of a human torso. The hard part was getting the ratios right because the sound had to travel through the foam at roughly the same speed as it travels through a real chest. It took many attempts, and she has said the failures were a large part of what she learned. When the judges at the Mott Million Dollar Challenge asked her to describe a trait of entrepreneurship she had demonstrated, she started talking about those failures.A better and cheaper stethoscopeDigital stethoscopes on the market often cost hundreds of dollars. That’s where Xu’s design stands out. The devices she designed are low-cost. They are so affordable that the flexible circuit board can be made in bulk for about one dollar. That difference matters most in places where clinics have little money to spend. Xu hopes Aucura will reach rural and underfunded areas, where medical care is already stretched thin. “This would allow it to reach areas where medical clinics might not be funded, since it’s relatively cheaper and would enable wider access to digital stethoscope technologies,” Xu added. Her long-term goal is for the device to become a standard tool in the field.After winning the entrepreneurship prize, Xu already has bigger plans for her future. She plans to study a STEM subject at university. “I’m really passionate about electrical engineering and biomedical engineering right now.” She also wants to continue developing Aucura so that it can reach the market. “I really hope that Aucura can be used in rural areas or less-funded areas, where they might not have access to that many resources. The end goal of Aucura is for it to be ubiquitous, like a new standard in auscultation technology.”

articles.title: Estrela morta pode antecipar futuro do Sistema Solar; entenda | G1
articles.standfirst: Estrutura nunca observada antes ao redor de uma anã branca pode ser mantida por dois corpos que sobreviveram à morte da estrela, um deles possivelmente do tamanho de Plutão.
articles.summary: Astrônomos identificaram dois anéis de restos de planetas ao redor de uma anã branca, estrutura inédita que pode ser mantida por corpos que sobreviveram à estrela.
articles.body:
Ilustração mostra dois anéis de gás e poeira ao redor da anã branca J1328−1450. — Foto: ESO/L. Calçada

Astrônomos descobriram uma estrutura inédita ao redor de uma estrela morta do nosso Cosmos: dois anéis separados formados por restos de antigos corpos planetários.

O sistema fica em torno da anã branca J1328−1450 e pode ajudar os cientistas a entender o que acontece com planetas e outros corpos celestes depois que uma estrela semelhante ao Sol chega ao fim da vida.

A descoberta, publicada na revista "Nature Astronomy", foi feita com observações do Very Large Telescope (VLT), do Observatório Europeu do Sul (ESO), instalado no deserto do Atacama, no Chile.

🌟 ENTENDA: Uma anã branca é o núcleo extremamente denso que resta depois que uma estrela como o Sol esgota seu combustível, se expande e perde suas camadas externas.

Nesse processo, planetas próximos podem ser destruídos. Outros corpos conseguem sobreviver, mas podem acabar fragmentados posteriormente, formando discos de poeira e gás ao redor da estrela.

No caso da J1328−1450 , porém, os astrônomos encontraram algo diferente.

Em vez de um único disco contínuo, os restos estão distribuídos em dois anéis de gás separados por um espaço bem definido. Segundo os autores, essa configuração nunca havia sido observada antes em torno de uma anã branca.

“Esta é a primeira observação de um sistema complexo com um disco duplo de restos e, potencialmente, dois planetesimais sobreviventes”, afirmou Nicola Gentile Fusillo, astrônomo da Universidade de Trieste, na Itália, e autor principal do estudo.

Corpos podem ter sobrevivido à morte da estrela

A principal hipótese dos pesquisadores é que dois corpos planetários ainda estejam orbitando a anã branca e ajudando a manter os dois anéis separados.

Esses objetos, contudo, não foram vistos diretamente. A existência deles foi proposta a partir da forma e do comportamento do gás observado ao redor da estrela.

O corpo mais próximo poderia ter o tamanho de um asteroide . Já o mais distante poderia ser comparável a Ceres, Plutão ou até à Lua, dependendo de sua composição e da distância exata em relação à estrela.

Segundo o estudo, a presença de dois corpos em órbitas diferentes também ajudaria a explicar por que o gás permanece concentrado em duas regiões distintas, sem preencher o espaço entre elas.

Os astrônomos encontraram ainda diferenças na composição dos dois anéis.

O anel mais próximo da estrela é rico em magnésio , enquanto o mais distante apresenta muito menos desse elemento. Para os pesquisadores, isso pode indicar que os restos vieram de dois corpos planetários diferentes.

Outra possibilidade é que tenham origem em partes distintas de um mesmo objeto, como camadas internas e externas de um antigo planeta ou corpo rochoso.

Além do magnésio, foram identificados elementos como cálcio, oxigênio e ferro. A composição geral é semelhante à de materiais rochosos encontrados na parte interna do nosso Sistema Solar.

Ilustração mostra os dois anéis de gás e poeira ao redor da anã branca J1328−1450, possivelmente mantidos por corpos que sobreviveram à morte da estrela. — Foto: Fortuna e Gentile Fusillo

O que isso tem a ver com o futuro do Sistema Solar?

O sistema pode funcionar como uma espécie de retrato de uma fase muito distante do futuro do nosso próprio Sistema Solar.

Daqui a bilhões de anos, o Sol também deve se transformar em uma anã branca . Antes disso, vai se expandir e alterar profundamente o sistema ao seu redor, podendo destruir os planetas mais próximos.

Parte dos corpos que sobreviverem a essa transformação poderá continuar orbitando o que restar do Sol. Ao longo do tempo, colisões e outras interações podem fragmentá-los e espalhar seus restos ao redor da estrela.

É justamente um cenário desse tipo que os astrônomos acreditam estar observando em J1328−1450 .

“Este sistema oferece uma visão notável de como poderá ser o futuro dos sistemas planetários, incluindo sistemas como o nosso”, afirmou Felipe Lagos-Vilches, coautor do estudo.

A descoberta também mostra que o fim de um sistema planetário pode ser mais complexo do que se imaginava.

Segundo os pesquisadores, a estrutura em anéis encontrada ao redor da estrela morta lembra formações observadas em discos ao redor de estrelas jovens , onde planetas ainda estão se formando.

A semelhança sugere que processos capazes de organizar matéria em anéis podem atuar tanto no nascimento quanto nas etapas finais de sistemas planetários.

articles.title: Trump says he’ll roll back Biden-era methane rules for oil and gas companies
articles.summary: The EPA plans to ease regulations aimed at curbing methane leaks, Trump said. The potent greenhouse gas is a major contributor to climate change.
articles.body: President Donald Trump said Tuesday his administration plans to ease regulations on methane — a potent greenhouse gas that is the second-biggest contributor to climate change after carbon dioxide. Speaking at a midterm rally in Texas, Trump announced the rollback of methane emissions rules for oil and gas producers that the Biden administration finalized in 2024. “Tonight, I’m officially terminating Biden’s expensive and unnecessary methane regulations to save consumers and energy producers,” Trump said, adding that Democrats had “crushed small oil and gas operators” with excessive regulation. He did not provide further details. The Environmental Protection Agency previewed the changes this month, promising to loosen regulations on methane leaks at lower-production oil wells, among other changes. EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin said at the time: “Americans must be able to afford to heat their homes in the winter and fill up their car and drive to work. They can’t do that when the people producing the energy are weighed down by unnecessary burdens.” Trump made the announcement just a week before the midterm elections, in which numerous polls show that high fuel costs are a key issue for many voters. Methane, the main component of natural gas, traps more heat in the atmosphere than carbon dioxide, though it also breaks down more quickly. Scientists consider methane to be about 80 times more potent than carbon dioxide over 20 years. Methane, which is also released from natural sources like wetlands, is responsible for roughly one-third of all global warming. The Biden administration viewed eliminating methane leaks from oil and gas production as a relatively quick way to drive down emissions. The low-producing wells the rollback would affect (also called stripper wells) produce about 7% to 8% of U.S. natural gas, but they could account for about 50% of the methane that leaks into the atmosphere, research suggests. Many of those wells are near the end of their lives or at risk of falling below the threshold of profitability. However, the National Stripper Well Association has been calling for the rollback, saying in a letter last month that “the costs associated with complying with these regulations will make the wells uneconomical to operate.” As part of the rollback, the EPA also plans to eliminate its Super Emitter Program, which aimed to create a system for third-party groups to report methane leaks from natural gas production. Such leaks cannot be easily seen with the naked eye, but they can be detected by satellites or special thermal imaging cameras. The Trump administration paused implementing the program last year. Now, it is seeking to shutter it. Environmental and health groups decried the rollbacks, saying they would increase pollution in the atmosphere and increase the effects of climate change. Liz Scott, a senior director of national advocacy for the American Lung Association, said any rollback of methane regulations would also increase air pollution from volatile organic compounds, which are released alongside leaking methane during oil and gas production. “The pollution that’s released alongside methane carries immediate health harms, particularly for communities living near oil and gas sites,” Scott told NBC News. “When you roll back protections on the leaking or flaring of methane, you’re also going to roll back the protections that communities rely on for those air pollutants.” David Doniger, a senior attorney for the Natural Resources Defense Council, said methane leaks were one of the “dumbest” forms of pollution because the industry was losing the product it was selling and hurting the planet in the process. “The industry doesn’t pay attention to leaks that it should,” Doniger told NBC News. “They would make more money capturing this stuff and piping it to the point of sale than by losing it.” Before the rollbacks can take effect, they must go through an EPA rulemaking process that includes a public comment period. If a final rule is implemented, the EPA could then face legal challenges, including challenges from a coalition of environmental groups that includes the NRDC. “I would expect it to be another lawsuit,” Doniger said. The methane rollback is part of the Trump administration’s systematic effort to eliminate regulations designed to fight climate change. In February, the EPA repealed emissions rules for vehicles, which account for the most carbon pollution in the U.S. It announced last month that it would roll back emissions limits on coal- and gas-fired power plants. It has even upended its own endangerment finding, a legal decision that says greenhouse gases are warming the Earth in a way that threatens public health and welfare. Zeldin has described his agenda as an effort to “drive a dagger through the heart of climate-change religion.” The effects of climate change are becoming increasingly severe. Much of the globe baked in extreme heat this summer: The months from June through August were the warmest ever recorded for the contiguous U.S. Last year was the third-hottest in modern history, according to Copernicus, the European Union’s climate monitoring service. The past 11 years have been the 11 warmest on record, Copernicus data shows.

articles.title: A 1,600-year-old Roman cup turns green or ruby red depending on how light hits it; after years of experiments, Sheffield researchers have recreated the glass effect using tiny gold and silver particles
articles.summary: A drinking cup made around 1,600 years ago has a remarkable property: it can appear green when light falls on it and ruby red when light shines through it.
articles.body: A drinking cup made around 1,600 years ago has a remarkable property: it can appear green when light falls on it and ruby red when light shines through it. Now, researchers at the University of Sheffield have recreated the unusual glass effect, offering a new understanding of the technique used by ancient Roman glassmakers.According to the official website of University of Sheffield, the team has successfully reproduced the effect of the famous Lycurgus Cup using a repeatable glass recipe. The original artifact, held at the British Museum, is made from a special type of glass known as ‘dichroic glass,’ which displays different colours depending on how light interacts with it.The achievement follows extensive experiments by Dr Lisa Hollands, a technician in the university’s School of Chemical, Materials and Biological Engineering, working with Professor Caroline Jackson, an expert in Roman glass.Why does the Roman cup change colour?The British Museum dates the Lycurgus Cup to the fourth century AD. Its collection record identifies it as a Late Roman drinking cup made of glass, with silver-gilt fittings around its rim and base. The cup’s green-to-red colour change is linked to tiny amounts of gold and silver in the glass. According to the University of Sheffield, these metals formed nanoparticles, particles thousands of times smaller than a grain of sand that interact with light in unusual ways.When light reflects off the cup, the glass appears jade green. When light passes through it, the glass takes on a ruby-red appearance. The effect depends on the position of the light source and the way the glass absorbs and scatters different wavelengths of light. The nanoparticles are smaller than the wavelengths of visible light, and their size and shape affect the colours observed. The precise composition and formation of these particles are important to producing the distinctive effect.The Lycurgus Cup is particularly notable because it is the only surviving example of a Roman glass cage cup known to display this exceptional colour-changing behaviour, according to the University of Sheffield. Cage cups are elaborate vessels in which decorative glasswork is cut away from the body of the vessel, leaving figures and patterns connected by narrow bridges.Years of experiments to recreate an ancient techniqueThe team worked to study what was known about Roman glassmaking and develop a base glass using modern materials intended to mimic those available to ancient craftsmen. The greater challenge was getting small quantities of gold and silver into the glass in the right form. The team tested different furnaces, starting materials and oxygen levels. The experiments even included adding sugar to the mixture. Eventually, Hollands developed a recipe that produced glass appearing opaque green in reflected light and red when illuminated from behind.A modern sculpture inspired by the ancient cupAfter the initial glass was exhibited at LightFest, the researchers commissioned glass artist Elliot Walker to create a contemporary sculpture using Hollands’ recipe. Walker won season two of Netflix’s ‘Blown Away.’ The sculpture draws on the story depicted on the original cup and the form of the ancient Farnese Atlas sculpture. Walker explained that the design needed a blown-glass element to demonstrate the colour-changing effect clearly.The new work is scheduled to be unveiled at Sheffield’s Millennium Gallery during the University’s Festival of the Mind, running from November 6 to 15, 2026. The university says the sculpture will subsequently go on permanent display at its Turner Museum of Glass.What the research could mean beyond artThe recreated glass has immediate decorative potential, but the research also has wider scientific relevance. According to the University of Sheffield, the project forms part of work exploring materials that use light for applications in areas such as solar energy, quantum technologies and healthcare diagnostics. The knowledge gained may also contribute to the development of advanced glasses used to immobilise radioactive waste.The Lycurgus Cup itself remains at the British Museum. Its collection record describes the vessel as a fourth-century Roman drinking cup decorated with scenes from the story of Lycurgus, the mythical king of Thrace. In the myth shown on the cup, Lycurgus attacks Dionysus and his followers. Ambrosia, one of the god’s companions, is transformed into a vine that coils around and traps the king.The ancient vessel combines this elaborate decoration with an optical effect that still attracts scientific attention. By recreating its colour-changing glass, the Sheffield team has brought researchers closer to understanding how a technique used by Roman craftsmen can be reproduced with modern materials and scientific knowledge.

articles.title: Scientists collected DNA from seawater at 316 sites across Japan and found 126 fish species farther north than previously recorded, revealing how warming seas may be reshaping where coastal wildlife can survive
articles.summary: The waters surrounding Japan have been changing in ways that may not be immediately visible to the people who depend on them.
articles.body: The waters surrounding Japan have been changing in ways that may not be immediately visible to the people who depend on them. But one day the oceans may not look like before and may not inhabit the same species we are familiar with. According to Phys.org, a nationwide study of marine environmental DNA (eDNA) in Japan has found evidence of fish species appearing farther north than previously recorded. Scientists are turning to a disparate source of evidence to understand these changes: the DNA left behind in seawater.In a nationwide study, researchers analysed thousands of water samples collected along Japan's coastline, noting 126 fish species in locations farther north in previously recorded indications. The findings offer a closer look at how marine habitats may be changing as ocean temperatures rise, with potential consequences for fishing communities, local food traditions and the ecosystems that support coastal life.How a bucket of seawater can reveal marine lifeResearchers at the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST) conducted what the institution described as Japan's largest marine environmental DNA study. Published in the journal Diversity and Distributions on October 26, 2026, the research studied 2,672 seawater samples collected from 316 different locations along Japan's coastline between the years 2017 and 2024.The sampling technique used in the study, known as environmental DNA, or eDNA examines how fish leave traces of genetic material in their surroundings by shedding of their skin, scales and the deposition of other biological matter. By collecting seawater and extracting the DNA it contains, researchers can compare the resulting sequences with reference DNA data to identify the species likely to be present in a particular area without having to directly capture or observe each marine animal. According to OIST, Japan's extensive sequencing of local marine fauna and the development of the MiFish primers in Japan has helped improve the coverage and accuracy in detection of species.This approach offers a practical way to study marine biodiversity across extensive stretches of coastline. The research team, led by first author Ayşe Haruka Oshima Açıkbaş, a former doctoral student at OIST, combined nearly 1,000 newly collected samples with existing data. The resulting dataset helped researchers examine fish distributions across Japan in greater detail, including locations where previous observations had been limited.What warmer oceans could mean for Japan's coastal communitiesWith global warming and climate change affecting marine habitats, rising ocean temperatures may be contributing to shifts in the ranges of species towards cooler waters. The eDNA sampling method can help inform further research into the societal and environmental implications of these changing seascapes in Japan.For Japan, where fishing is closely connected to food, regional identity and local economies, the changes in the ocean and the marine could extend beyond the study of marine biology itself. Fish that have traditionally been caught in particular regions may become less common, while species unfamiliar to local fishing communities could begin appearing more frequently.Timothy Ravasi, head of OIST's Marine Climate Change Unit and a senior author of the study noted that fishermen across Japan have already observed differences in their catches as compared to previous decades. He further highlighted the difficulties that unfamiliar fish can create for small, family-run fishing businesses that may need to adapt their equipment, techniques and knowledge in accordance with new species.The fish appearing farther north could affect marine ecosystems tooThe study has further identified commercially important species among those recorded beyond their previously documented northern ranges including Japanese scad and blacktip grouper. Another species identified was the black rabbitfish (S. fuscescens), which is suspected of contributing to the irrecoverable damage to seaweed beds, a phenomenon known in Japan as isoyake. Such seaweed beds have provided important habitats for marine organisms, making changes in the distribution of species that feed on them relevant to wider ecosystem health. The findings therefore raise questions about how changing fish distributions across the ocean can influence the relationship between species, the condition of the coastal habitats and the communities that depend on them.As more samples are collected, environmental DNA databases could help researchers identify emerging patterns, compare observations across years and improve their understanding of where marine species are being detected. The research team has also identified predictive modelling as a potential direction for future work, moving beyond recording the presence or absence of DNA towards investigating why certain species appear in particular locations. By examining DNA traces in seawater, scientists are developing another way to follow these changes, offering a clearer picture of how Japan's marine environments may be responding to a warming world.

articles.title: Tras más de 160 años de excavaciones en Troya, aparece su primer instrumento musical: una flauta de hace 2.800 años
articles.standfirst: El empresario canadiense aconseja ayudar a las pymes a usar la IA y construir centros de datos
articles.summary: El empresario canadiense aconseja ayudar a las pymes a usar la IA y construir centros de datos
articles.body: Durante más de un siglo y medio, Troya ha revelado murallas, palacios, cerámicas y tesoros, pero nunca había ofrecido una pista tangible de cómo sonaba. Ahora, por fin, los arqueólogos han encontrado su primer instrumento musical: una flauta de hueso de unos 2.800 años de antigüedad. El hallazgo se ha producido en la colina de Hisarlik, en la provincia turca de Çanakkale, donde se levanta el yacimiento declarado Patrimonio Mundial por la UNESCO. Según el Ministerio de Cultura y Turismo de Turquía, se trata de la primera prueba arqueológica directa de una cultura musical en la ciudad. La pieza apareció en niveles del periodo arcaico y se ha fechado en torno al siglo VIII a. C., una época cercana a la que se atribuye la composición de la 'Ilíada'. Los investigadores han recuperado un fragmento del instrumento que conserva la cabeza unida al cuerpo, un detalle que permitirá estudiar su estructura y su funcionamiento. Las excavaciones están dirigidas por Rüstem Aslan, de la Universidad Onsekiz Mart de Çanakkale, que ha subrayado que es el primer y único instrumento musical localizado desde que comenzaron los trabajos en el yacimiento, en la segunda mitad del siglo XIX. Además, los objetos fabricados con materiales orgánicos, como el hueso, rara vez sobreviven tanto tiempo, lo que aumenta el valor del descubrimiento. La flauta no es especialmente antigua si se compara con otros instrumentos de hueso: en Europa se han hallado ejemplares del Paleolítico con más de 40.000 años de antigüedad. Su importancia reside en el lugar donde ha aparecido y en lo que revela sobre la vida cotidiana de quienes habitaron Troya. En el mundo antiguo, los instrumentos de viento, como la siringa o flauta de pan, se empleaban en celebraciones y rituales, algunos vinculados al culto a Dioniso. Por eso, los expertos confían en que esta flauta ayude a entender mejor el papel de la música en la sociedad troyana. Junto a la flauta, el equipo ha desenterrado también la cabeza de un ídolo de forma humana de unos 4.500 años, hallada en la zona de la puerta de Troya II. Según Aslan, apenas se han encontrado entre tres y cinco piezas similares en toda la historia de las excavaciones.

articles.title: La seta que hace ver personas diminutas: identifican la especie, pero su sustancia sigue siendo un misterio
articles.standfirst: Estas visiones se habrían sido descritas por individuos de China y Filipinas
articles.summary: Estas visiones se habrían sido descritas por individuos de China y Filipinas
articles.body: No es la primera vez que un grupo de individuos relata cómo tras ingerir una seta, acaba visionando todo tipo de alucinaciones. No obstante, sí puede ser la primera ocasión en la que no se logra identificar qué sustancia del hongo es la que lo provoca. La Universidad de Utah sigue estudiando estos hongos para encontrar respuestas. La especie que provoca dichas alucinaciones es la Lanmaoa asiática. Es por eso que los principales testimonios provienen de individuos de China y Filipinas. Según cuentan, tras ingerir esta seta, las personas vieron diferentes figuras humanas vestidas con ropa muy brillante y bailando, como si formaran parte del mundo real. Los investigadores le han dado nombre a estas alucinaciones. Basándose en la novela de ‘Los viajes de Gulliver’, se les han llamado liliputienses, es decir, es un guiño a Liliput, la tierra ficticia en la que vivían los seres diminutos de la obra. Todos los ciudadanos que han experimentado estas alucinaciones, describen que ven a personas del tamaño de unos gnomos con ropas coloridas. La cuestión aquí es que ningún científico ha conseguido identificar qué sustancia es la que provocan dichas visiones. En un momento dado, incluso se llegó a dudar de que fuera esta especie de hongos lo que produjese estas alucinaciones. Aunque, en las últimas décadas, se ha vuelto a buscar respuestas a base de pruebas a la Lanmaoa asiática. El estudio identificó 17 especies del género Lanmaoa en 53 ejemplares, cuatro de ellas nuevas para la ciencia. Aunque se ha descubierto el hongo relacionado con las visiones de pequeñas figuras humanas en China y Filipinas, todavía se desconoce qué sustancia causa este efecto y si es el mismo hongo que originó los nuevos casos descritos en Papúa Nueva Guinea.

articles.title: Scientists spot rare tiny snakes in Malaysia that do not just slither but do cartwheels; they roll at 12 feet per second when they sense danger
articles.summary: Scientists have captured rare footage of tiny Southeast Asian snakes performing rapid cartwheels to escape danger, revealing an unusual form of movement
articles.body: Scientists have captured rare footage of tiny Southeast Asian snakes performing rapid cartwheels to escape danger, revealing an unusual form of movement that allows the reptiles to travel at speeds of up to 12 feet per second. The findings, published in Current Biology on October 19, 2026, were reported by Science News, Live Science and Japan’s Toho University, whose researchers investigated how the snakes coordinate their bodies during the remarkable manoeuvre. The behaviour, known as active cartwheeling, has been documented in dwarf reed snakes belonging to the genus Pseudorabdion. Unlike conventional snake movement, which relies on lateral undulation along the ground, this escape technique involves the animal briefly lifting parts of its body into the air and rolling forward in a series of rapid rotations. The research offers a closer look at how these small, secretive reptiles manage the unusual feat while keeping their heads relatively stable and maintaining control over their direction of travel.How do the snakes perform their cartwheels?Researchers from Japan and Malaysia studied 13 dwarf reed snakes from three Pseudorabdion species, alongside six related reed snakes from the genus Calamaria. They built a narrow track measuring approximately 2.2 metres and recorded the animals using cameras positioned above and beside it. The footage revealed a carefully coordinated sequence. The snake begins by curling its body into a C shape, lifting its head and pointing it in the direction it intends to move. It then straightens its body and pushes off the ground, briefly lifting part of itself into the air.As it becomes airborne, the snake twists its body into an arch and swings it forward past its head. When the body makes contact with the ground again, the movement initiates another roll. By alternating the side of its body that touches down, the snake can repeat the sequence and continue moving forward. Despite these rapid rotations, the researchers found that the snake's head remains relatively stable and aligned with its direction of travel. This control may help it maintain its orientation and move along a narrow path without losing its bearings.Cartwheeling snakes can reach speeds of 12 feet per secondThe researchers measured peak forward speeds ranging from 1.72 to 3.69 metres per second, equivalent to approximately 5.6 to 12.1 feet per second, or around 6 to 13 kilometres per hour. The fastest recorded movement was roughly four times the peak forward speed measured when the snakes travelled using conventional side-to-side undulation.All 13 snakes belonging to the Pseudorabdion genus demonstrated the rolling behaviour during the experiments. None of the six Calamaria snakes used the same technique under the test conditions, suggesting that the behaviour may be specific to certain groups rather than a universal ability among small reed snakes.However, the findings do not establish that cartwheeling is the fastest or most effective escape method in every situation. The tests measured movement along a controlled track, and researchers still need to determine how the snakes use the technique in their natural habitats.Why do these snakes roll instead of slither?Dwarf reed snakes are small, secretive reptiles that spend much of their time beneath leaf litter, fallen branches and other ground cover. Their behaviour is consistent with an animal that relies on avoiding danger rather than confronting larger predators. Scientists suspect that sudden, rapid rolling could help the snakes escape threats, potentially startling or confusing a predator long enough to reach shelter. Some researchers have also suggested that the unusual movement might disrupt scent trails, although this possibility remains unproven.The behaviour was first formally documented in a 2023 study published in Biotropica. Researchers described a dwarf reed snake rolling away after being startled during fieldwork in Malaysia. The new study builds on that initial observation by examining the mechanics of the movement in greater detail.Although rolling locomotion is unusual in the animal kingdom, it is not entirely unique. The Moroccan flic-flac spider, for example, uses a rolling movement to escape threats. The snake study nevertheless offers a rare example of how an animal without limbs can use coordinated body rotations to achieve rapid forward movement.Researchers must also determine how much energy the movement requires, how long the snakes can sustain it and whether specific anatomical or neurological features enable them to perform the manoeuvre. For now, the findings demonstrate that snake locomotion can be more varied than conventional slithering suggests. By coordinating rapid body rotations while stabilising their heads, these small reptiles have developed an unusual way to move quickly when threatened.

articles.title: Priscilla Chan-backed Biohub's researchers used AI and CRISPR to identify new psoriasis drug targets; topical gels successfully  worked in mice
articles.summary: Researchers at Biohub, an organisation backed by the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative co-founded by Priscilla Chan, have identified potential new drug targets
articles.body: Researchers at Biohub, an organisation backed by the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative co-founded by Priscilla Chan, have identified potential new drug targets for psoriasis by combining AI with genetic screening. The study, published in Nature Communications, discovered 2 biological pathways that could help control the skin inflammation associated with this chronic condition. When researchers developed topical gels targeting these pathways and tested them in mice, the treatments reduced disease severity and produced results comparable to an existing injected therapy, opening a possible route towards more localised treatment.How AI and CRISPR revealed new psoriasis drug targetsThe research, led by Shana Kelley, president of Biohub, and Abdalla M. Abdrabou, leader of its Functional Immunogenomics group, focused on keratinocytes. These are the main cells in the outer layer of the skin and play a central role in the development of psoriasis lesions.According to the Biohub, the researchers wanted to understand how inflammation begins in these cells and identify ways to interrupt it without affecting the immune system more broadly.To investigate this, the team used CRISPR, a genetic editing technology that allows scientists to disable individual genes and observe the effects. The researchers examined approximately 19,000 genes in human skin cells using a library of around 77,000 guide RNAs. They then measured changes in IL17RA, a protein that helps skin cells respond to inflammatory signals associated with psoriasis.The experiment identified hundreds of genes that influenced IL17RA levels. However, determining which discoveries were genuinely new required another layer of analysis.As explained in the Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine report, the team developed an AI tool called VirtualCRISPR to compare the experimental findings with existing scientific literature and prioritise genes that had received little attention in previous research.Two promising pathways emerged from the screeningThe AI-guided analysis highlighted 2 genes with potential for drug development, ALOX5 and OXTR. Both had limited previous connections to the regulation of IL17RA in skin cells.ALOX5 produces an enzyme involved in inflammatory processes. It is already targeted by zileuton, a drug approved by the US FDA for treating asthma.The second target, OXTR, produces the receptor through which oxytocin acts. Oxytocin is widely associated with childbirth and social bonding, but its receptor has not been established as a significant regulator of psoriasis-related skin inflammation.The researchers identified cligosiban as a compound that blocks this receptor.According to the study published in Nature Communications, experiments in human skin cells showed that interfering with either pathway reduced IL17RA levels and lowered the production of inflammatory substances.The team also used 3D skin cultures to investigate how the compounds affected skin tissue. These models reproduce important features of human skin and helped researchers examine the effects of the treatments more closely.Topical gels reduced inflammation in miceAfter identifying the targets, the researchers reformulated zileuton and cligosiban into gels that could be applied directly to the skin. They then tested the treatments in mice with psoriasis-like inflammation.The results were encouraging. As reported by Biohub, both gels reduced disease severity within 5 days. By the 7th day, their effects were comparable to those of an injected anti-IL17RA drug used as a comparison in the experiment.The treated mice also showed improvements in skin thickness, which had increased because of inflammation. Cligosiban produced particularly broad improvements in the restoration of skin characteristics.The findings suggest that targeting the skin cells involved in psoriasis may help control the condition without requiring drugs to act throughout the body. However, the experiments were conducted in mice, not people. The findings demonstrate potential rather than an established treatment for patients.Importance of these findings for future treatmentPsoriasis affects more than 125 million people worldwide, according to the research published in Nature Communications. Existing treatments can help manage the condition, but some options have limitations.Mild cases can often be managed with topical treatments, including steroid creams. People with moderate-to-severe psoriasis may need medicines that act throughout the body, including biologic drugs that target immune signalling proteins. These treatments can be expensive, require injections and carry risks associated with suppressing immune activity.Researchers hope topical formulations could eventually provide effective treatment with fewer effects beyond the affected skin.Biohub's wider inflammation research programme aims to understand how inflammatory processes develop and change inside human tissues. The psoriasis study also demonstrates how AI can help scientists make better use of large experimental datasets.
